[Modular programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_programming)
splits a program into separate **modules**,
each of which does one job and can be understood, tested and changed on its own.
In R and Python, a module can be a function, a file or a package.
Splitting a problem into such parts is called
[decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decomposition_(computer_science)).
Guides to scientific computing recommend it:
@wilson2014best advise modularizing code rather than copying and pasting it,
and @wilson2017good advise decomposing programs into functions.

Each module has an **interface** and an **implementation**.
The interface is what other code may rely on:
for an R function, its name, arguments and return value;
for a package, its exported functions [@wickham2023rpkgs].
The implementation is everything else.
Code that calls a module depends only on its interface,
so the smaller the interface,
the more of the module you can change without changing that code.

Two properties describe how well a program is divided [@stevens1974structured]:

- **Cohesion** is how closely the parts inside one module belong together.
  Aim for high cohesion:
  a file that cleans one dataset is more cohesive
  than a `utils.R` file that holds every helper in the project.
- **Coupling** is how strongly one module depends on another,
  for example on its internal details or on shared global state.
  Aim for low coupling:
  a script that calls a function from another file
  is less coupled than one that `source()`s that file
  and then uses the intermediate objects it created.

### Decide what each module hides

@parnas1972criteria described two ways to split the same program into modules.
One split followed the steps of the program in order.
The other gave each module one design decision that was likely to change,
such as a file format or a data structure,
and hid that decision behind the module's interface.
Parnas argued that the second split is easier to change,
because a change to one of those decisions touches only one module.
This approach is called **information hiding**.

In a data analysis, decisions that often change include:

- the format and location of the raw data;
- how a variable is coded or cleaned;
- which model is fitted.

Give each decision its own function or file.
For example, suppose that only `read_survey_data()` knows that the survey arrives as a CSV file:

```r
read_survey_data <- function(path) {
  readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
}
```

If the survey later moves into a database,
you change only `read_survey_data()`,
and the code that calls it keeps working:

```r
raw_data <- read_survey_data(here::here("data", "survey.csv"))
clean_data <- clean_survey_data(raw_data)
model <- fit_coverage_model(clean_data)
```

### When to make something a module

A useful test is whether you can state the code's job in one sentence
and name its inputs and outputs.
If you can, it is a candidate for its own function.
Move a set of functions into a package
only once several projects use them,
since a package adds documentation, tests and releases to maintain
(see [Complete Package Development Workflow](#sec-r-workflow)).
